Healthcare AI Hackathon
Join OpenAI, AWS, JPM, Troutman Pepper, Pear VC, NEA, and Cathay Innovation for a one-day healthcare AI hackathon bringing together engineers, clinicians, researchers, designers, and founders to build products that solve real problems across health.
Why Attend?
🏆 Compete for up to $5,000 in first/second/third place cash prizes, advisory meetings with leading healthcare AI operators and industry sponsors, and 1:1 pitch opportunities with PearX, NEA, and Cathay

🚀 Connect with leaders from OpenAI, AWS, Stanford Medicine, J.P. Morgan, and leading VC-backed healthcare startups

🤝 Meet investors, founders, and operators shaping the future of healthcare

🏥 Collaborate with clinicians, engineers, researchers, designers, and entrepreneurs

Presented by Pear VC · NEA · Cathay Innovation
Powered by OpenAI · AWS · J.P. Morgan · Troutman Pepper
Healthcare is the largest industry in the world, yet much of its infrastructure still runs on fragmented software, manual workflows, and administrative overhead. Recent advances in foundation models and AI agents have created an opportunity to rethink how healthcare is delivered, from the clinician desktop to the insurance back office to the patient experience.
Life sciences is entering a similar inflection point, as advances in foundation models, biological data, and increasingly automated experimentation begin to reshape how we understand and engineer biology. From target discovery and molecular design to clinical development, AI is creating new ways to compress the traditional drug development cycle and build entirely new categories of therapeutics and research tools.
Throughout the day you'll work directly with venture investors, startup founders, physicians, and operators who spend every day building healthcare companies.
Teams will leave with relationships, recruiting opportunities, and potentially the foundation for their next startup.
Whether you're already building in healthcare or just discovering the space, you'll spend the day working on problems that matter.
What Should You Build?
Build something that meaningfully improves health.
We're less interested in incremental AI wrappers and more interested in products that unlock new capabilities, create new business models, or solve long-standing problems across the healthcare and life sciences ecosystem.
Some areas we're especially excited about include:
🧬 Care Delivery & Clinical Innovation
Build AI that makes care more accessible, personalized, and effective , from diagnostics and specialty care to home-based care, clinical trials, robotics, and entirely new models of care delivery.

🏥 Healthcare Infrastructure & Financing
Build AI that fixes the systems behind healthcare , improving how care is financed, administered, coordinated, and delivered across providers, payers, employers, marketplaces, and supply chains.

🔬 AI × Life Sciences
Build AI that better predicts what will actually happen in biology , using richer, multi-compartment data to model real-world outcomes such as toxicity, delivery, efficacy, and clinical trial endpoints rather than focusing only on molecular binding.

These are examples, not constraints. If you have a compelling idea that improves healthcare, feel free to build it because we want to see it!

About Event

WHAT IS re:AGENT

re:AGENT is a two-day build weekend focused on the infrastructure scientific agents still need: better datasets, sharper tools, and reliable ways to evaluate their work. Participants will use Paperclip , Proto , Claude , and other scientific AI tools to build systems that can take on real scientific problems and produce results worth trusting.
Paperclip turns papers, datasets, clinical trials, and biological databases into an agent-native workspace that AI systems can search, synthesize, and build upon. Proto is a design framework and infrastructure layer for generative biology, allowing builders to combine AI models and search for DNA, RNA, or protein sequences that satisfy custom criteria.
The weekend brings together engineers, scientists, computational biologists, founders, and AI researchers. Projects might include assembling a research-ready dataset that would be impractical to create by hand, along with the analysis needed to show that its findings are real. Others might involve designing a new biological system to a defined specification and testing whether it holds up against existing evidence.
The aim is not just to accelerate existing workflows, but to create the tools, datasets, and evaluation methods that make entirely new scientific questions and experiments possible.
READY TO BUILD?

If you're excited about the future of AI, agents and scientific discovery, we'll see you there...

People with the questions: scientists of all stripes. Wet lab, computational, clinical, industry. Biology, biochemistry, biophysics, chemistry, structural. Anyone with a real problem, ideally a real dataset, and the judgment to tell right from wrong results.

AI agents are easy to prototype and much harder to run in production. Once an agent touches real users, tools, data, budgets, and internal systems, the work becomes less about a clever prompt and more about routing, permissions, tracing, retries, evals, guardrails, cost controls, and deployment.
Join TrueFoundry and HackerSquad for a full-day Agent Harness hackathon focused on building production-minded agentic applications with TrueForge . The goal is simple: take an agent use case from idea or prototype toward something that can be observed, governed, evaluated, and operated.
TrueFoundry's AI Gateway, Agent Gateway, and MCP Gateway will frame the day. Builders will work on practical agent harness patterns such as model routing, controlled tool access, MCP workflows, observability, eval loops, fallback behavior, budget controls, governance, and deployment paths.
This is a technical builder event, not a passive product pitch. Bring a laptop, a strong use case, and a willingness to build under realistic production constraints.
What You Can Build
An agent workflow with model routing, retries, and fallback behavior

A tool-using agent with controlled MCP or API access

An observability layer for traces, tool calls, latency, usage, cost, and failures

An eval or test harness for agent behavior across repeated runs

A governance pattern for permissions, approvals, logging, blocking, or escalation

A deployment-minded agent application that shows how it would run inside a real team or platform environment

Why This Gets Hard in Production
Agent systems need to coordinate models, tools, permissions, memory, context, retries, and fallbacks without becoming brittle one-off glue code.

Teams need traces, audit logs, usage visibility, cost attribution, and eval loops so they can understand what an agent did, why it did it, and what changed between runs.

Scaling agents means managing quotas, budgets, latency, provider failures, tool access, and security policies across teams.

Guardrails need to become runtime controls: clear rules for what data an agent can see, which tools it can call, which actions require human approval, and how unsafe requests or outputs get blocked, logged, or escalated.

Deployment gets harder when agents need to connect to internal systems, respect governance rules, and stay reliable as usage grows.

About Event

Build It. Test It. Prove It.
Smells like a hackathon. Runs like a pressure test, on you, not just your idea.
Proving Ground runs a three-day Sprint where judges push past the pitch. No script survives real questions about what you tried, what broke, and what you changed.
Past teams have gone on to raise from 500 Global and Blitzscaling Ventures, and been accepted into Berkeley SkyDeck and Confluent's accelerator, independently, without Proving Ground's involvement in those decisions.
What this is
A hackathon judges what you built by the end. We watch during the process and look past the end to what may come next.

The team is almost everything. How you make decisions under pressure, how you handle a setback, how you treat each other when something breaks. You'll document that as you go. What we ask you to show and how we question it are built around behavior, not performance.
How it works
Over three days, founders build under real constraint. No script, no rehearsed demo. Judges probe what you tried, what broke, and what you changed, and compare where you started to where you ended.
Two Tracks
Discovery Track. Pre-market, no active customer contact yet. For the startup curious, including enterprise folks seriously exploring a leap.
Pre-seed Track. In-market, already talking to customers. Ship something real, show what's changed, pressure-test your next move.
After the Sprint
Select teams get invited into the Street Test: 30 days back in the real world, no artificial deadline, no audience. This is where we see if momentum was real or borrowed from the room. It's the part a hackathon can't offer, because a hackathon ends when the weekend does.

Media is becoming iterative.
For a century, a film was a finished thing. Made once, shipped once, watched. That is ending. The new model is media that gets made, remixed, and reshaped continuously, by small teams using tools that turn an idea into a finished frame in an afternoon.
Film is one of the biggest mediums this reshapes, and we want to bring the people rebuilding it in one room.
This September we're hosting a generative AI short film hackathon in San Francisco, with Machine Cinema, the most active community of AI filmmakers working today.
The format is simple. About 20 teams of three or four. A few hours to make and premiere a one to three minute animated short, using the latest tooling across video, image, audio, and world models.
A medium doesn't move forward in essays about it. It moves forward when the people defining it are in the same room, making things.
Come build with us!

candidates.title: The Next Interface Hackathon: Rethink how we talk to AI
candidates.evidence:
The Next Interface Hackathon: Rethink how we talk to AI
For three years, using AI meant typing into a box and waiting for text to come back.
That era is ending. 

The next interface isn't a chat window. It's worn, spoken, and always on.
Glasses that listen.
A pendant that remembers. 
A tracker you never charge. 
A second self that watches your screen and acts before you ask.
We're putting the founders building that future in one room with the people who want to build on it.

Half a day in San Francisco. 

Real hardware on the table. Working demos, not slideware.
The lineup is a short list of founders shipping the wearables that are pulling AI off the screen. 

The founders in the room:
Adam Cohen Hillel, Secondly - a personal AI "second self" that sees your screen and acts across every app you use. The chat box becomes a presence.
Nik Shevchenko, Omi - the open-source AI wearable necklace, with 250+ developer apps already built on it. Always listening, always yours.
AnhPhu Nguyen, Mira - AI smart glasses with no camera. They hear what you hear, recall every name, and translate 60+ languages in under a second. AnhPhu is the Harvard builder behind last year's viral I-XRAY demo.
Andy Kong, Chargerless - a 7-gram health tracker powered by daylight. One minute of sun a day and it never needs a charger.
What you'll build: pick a device, an API, or a live sensor stream. 

Ship something a person could actually wear or talk to by the time we demo.

 The strongest builds demo to the founders in the room.
This is for builders, hardware hackers, AI engineers, and designers who think the keyboard is a temporary technology.
